\ifelse{html}{\href{https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental}{\figure{lifecycle-experimental.svg}{options: alt='[Experimental]'}}}{\strong{[Experimental]}}

`goldfish` usually models one dependent process at a time: `estimate_dynam()`
and `estimate_rem()` each take a single [make_specification()] object. Some
questions need more than one process modeled *together* -- for example, DyNES
(Dynamic Network Event/State models) asks how a panel-observed relational
state (survey waves) and a time-stamped relational-event stream co-evolve, with
the panel process's latent between-wave path *augmented* from the observed
waves. That joint model needs a specification portraying several co-evolving
processes at once, evaluated against one shared clock and process state --
`make_joint_specification()`.

This vignette covers what ships **today**: composing process specifications,
reading the extended `process_map`, and how coupling and separability are
detected. The estimator that actually fits a DyNES model, `estimate_dynes()`,
and the data-augmentation path that lets a panel layer be *modeled* (not just
read as a covariate), ship in later, still-in-development changes. What is
here is the substrate they are built on: this package version does not export
an estimator for the objects this vignette builds.

# Step 0: Load the package and data


``` r
library(goldfish)
library(manynet)
data("social_evolution")
social_evolution
#> # A tibble: 84 × 4
#>   label    active floor gradeType
#>   <chr>    <lgl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Actor 47 TRUE       4         3
#> 2 Actor 57 TRUE       2         1
#> 3 Actor 9  TRUE       9         2
#> 4 Actor 68 TRUE       8         1
#> 5 Actor 23 TRUE       5         2
#> 6 Actor 49 TRUE       7         4
#> # ℹ 78 more rows
#> # A tibble: 1,205 × 5
#>    from    to time                weight layer     
#>   <int> <int> <dttm>               <dbl> <chr>     
#> 1     1    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 2     2    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 3     3    67 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 4     4    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 5     5    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 6     6    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> # ℹ 1,199 more rows
```

`social_evolution` carries two layers over one node set of 84 actors: `calls`
(time-stamped phone calls, an `"event"` layer) and `friendship` (survey
nominations, a `"panel"` layer) -- see `vignette("teaching1")` for how it is
assembled. A multivariate specification needs **at least two** modeled
processes, so this vignette adds a second, synthetic `"event"` layer,
`meetings`, over the same actors -- purely illustrative, not a real measure of
anything in the Social Evolution study.


``` r
set.seed(1)
n_actors <- nrow(social_evolution$nodes)
n_meetings <- 40L
from_idx <- sample.int(n_actors, n_meetings, replace = TRUE)
to_idx <- (from_idx + sample.int(n_actors - 1, n_meetings, replace = TRUE) - 1) %%
  n_actors + 1L
meetings <- data.frame(
  from = from_idx,
  to = to_idx,
  time = sort(as.POSIXct("2008-09-09") + sort(sample(1:1e6, n_meetings))),
  weight = 1,
  layer = "meetings"
)

joint_data <- social_evolution
joint_data$ties <- rbind(as.data.frame(social_evolution$ties), meetings)
joint_data$info$directed <- c(joint_data$info$directed, meetings = TRUE)
joint_data$info$update <- c(joint_data$info$update, meetings = "increment")
joint_data$info$observation <- c(joint_data$info$observation, meetings = "event")
```

A layer is added to a `stocnet` object the same way regardless of how many
processes will model it: append its rows to `ties` and declare it in `info`
(`directed`, `update`, `observation`) -- exactly the metadata
`vignette("teaching1")`'s `add_info()` step records, just merged into an
existing object here instead of built fresh.

# Step 1: Specifying two co-evolving processes

Build one `specification.goldfish` per process with [make_specification()],
as for a single-process model, then combine them with
`make_joint_specification()`. `meetings`' choice formula reads
`tie(friendship)` -- a relational process reading the panel layer as a
covariate, which is exactly the kind of cross-process reference that makes
joining meaningful.


``` r
calls_spec <- make_specification(
  rate = ~ 1 + indeg,
  choice = ~ inertia + recip,
  layer = "calls",
  model = "DyNAM",
  data = joint_data
)

meetings_spec <- make_specification(
  rate = ~ 1 + outdeg,
  choice = ~ inertia + tie(friendship),
  layer = "meetings",
  model = "DyNAM",
  data = joint_data
)

joint_spec <- make_joint_specification(calls_spec, meetings_spec, data = joint_data)
joint_spec
#> ── <joint_specification.goldfish> ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 2 processes over one shared data object · 4 formulas · 0 coupled · 4 separable
#> · 0 auto-supplied
#> 
#> Layer "calls" — Model "DyNAM"
#> • Rate [fid 1, separable]: `~1 + indeg`
#> • Choice [fid 2, separable]: `~inertia + recip`
#> 
#> Layer "meetings" — Model "DyNAM"
#> • Rate [fid 3, separable]: `~1 + outdeg`
#> • Choice [fid 4, separable]: `~inertia + tie(friendship)`
#> 
#> ℹ Estimate a multivariate specification with
#> `estimate_dynes()`.
```

The print sections the composition per layer (flavors nested, when a layer has
them), names each formula's `fid` -- the integer id every downstream consumer
indexes by -- and marks whether it is `coupled` or `separable`.

A few construction rules worth knowing before combining processes of your own:

- **One focal layer per specification.** Each joined specification must model
  a *distinct* focal (dependent) layer; a layer's flavors cannot be split
  across two joined specifications. Reading a layer as a covariate is
  unrestricted, and reusing a layer that way across several specifications is
  exactly the coupling the join exists to portray.
- **One shared mode-map object.** All composed processes must be built over
  the same node universe. One- and two-mode processes may be joined, and
  dependent processes over *distinct* mode-pairs compose as long as every
  cross-process read conforms by *mode-set identity* -- the shared node space
  is a whole shared mode (e.g., a `{staff}x{director}` process and a
  `{director}x{project}` process sharing the whole `director` mode). A read
  bridging a mode subset to a larger union containing it does not conform and
  aborts at construction.
- **No panel layer is required.** Unlike an earlier iteration of this
  interface, construction does **not** require any process to reference a
  panel-observed layer. A combination referencing no panel layer at all still
  composes -- it is estimation-separable (each process's likelihood
  factorizes) but *generatively* coupled through the shared clock, so it
  remains a meaningful object once a generative consumer (a future
  `simulate()`) exists. Whether a composition is *estimable* as DyNES is a
  question for the estimator, not the constructor -- see Step 3.

# Step 2: Reading the `process_map`

The composed object carries an extended `process_map`: one row per
likelihood-producing formula across every composed process, unchanged in kind
from a single (possibly flavored) specification's, just with rows from every
process and one added column.


``` r
joint_spec$process_map
#>   fid    layer flavor family   stat_block has_intercept constraint_id coupled
#> 1   1    calls   <NA>   rate   DyNAM:rate          TRUE            NA   FALSE
#> 2   2    calls   <NA> choice DyNAM:choice         FALSE            NA   FALSE
#> 3   3 meetings   <NA>   rate   DyNAM:rate          TRUE            NA   FALSE
#> 4   4 meetings   <NA> choice DyNAM:choice         FALSE            NA   FALSE
```

- **`fid`** is the canonical integer identity for every downstream consumer
  (preprocessing, the walk handle, results) -- `layer`/`flavor` are rendered
  labels, never parsed back.
- **`stat_block`** is the dispatch family a formula's effects are deduplicated
  within (`model:sub_model`); a shared effect (say `tie(friendship)` read by
  two processes' choice formulas) is computed once per block, never across
  blocks.
- **`constraint_id`** is shared by a process's rate and choice when they carry
  the same support constraint.
- **`coupled`** is described next.

# Step 3: Coupling and separability

A fid is **coupled** iff its effects or support-constraint atoms *directly*
reference the state of a **modeled** panel layer -- a panel-observed layer
that is itself one of the joined processes' focal layers, so its between-wave
path is latent. Reading a panel layer that appears only as an **exogenous
covariate** -- modeled by none of the composed processes -- does not couple:
that covariate is a static step-covariate (its value jumps at wave times, not
augmented), so a fid reading it touches nothing latent.


``` r
joint_spec$process_map[, c("fid", "layer", "coupled")]
#>   fid    layer coupled
#> 1   1    calls   FALSE
#> 2   2    calls   FALSE
#> 3   3 meetings   FALSE
#> 4   4 meetings   FALSE
joint_spec$modeled_panel
#> character(0)
```

Here every fid is `coupled = FALSE`: `meetings`' choice reads `friendship`,
but `friendship` is panel-observed and modeled by *neither* composed process
(`joint_spec$modeled_panel` is empty), so it is a static covariate, not a
latent one. This is the **exogenous-only-panel** case -- it composes, but has
nothing latent to jointly estimate.

Making a fid coupled needs a **modeled panel layer** in the join -- a
specification whose focal layer is itself panel-observed, so its own
between-wave path is what augmentation would fill in. `make_specification()`
does not build one directly today: a panel-observed focal layer is rejected as
"SAOM/RSiena territory," matching goldfish's current event-stream estimators
(`estimate_dynam()` / `estimate_rem()`), which model event streams, not
between-wave states. The change that lifts that restriction and supplies the
augmented data path (`dynes-augmentation`) is still in development. Once a
join *does* carry a modeled panel process, every fid reading its state --
directly, through a support-constraint atom, or through a windowed effect --
is marked coupled, and the print sections separable fids apart so a mixed
specification's DyNES-estimable core is visible at a glance.

Separability is **not** simply "not coupled": a fid whose own focal layer is a
modeled panel process is never separable, even when its own formula reads
nothing -- its likelihood is over that layer's latent path, so it cannot be
estimated apart from the augmentation that fills it in. Reading (or not
reading) another modeled panel layer is what `coupled` tracks; a fid's own
layer being one is a separate, stronger condition.

# Step 4: What estimating a joint specification requires

`goldfish` does not yet export a multivariate estimator -- `estimate_dynes()`
ships in a later change (`abmcem`, with its data-augmentation path in
`dynes-augmentation`). What this version *does* enforce is that the
event-stream estimators refuse to silently mis-fit a joint object:


``` r
tryCatch(
  estimate_dynam(joint_spec, sub_model = "choice"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> [1] "A <joint_specification.goldfish> cannot be estimated with the\nevent-stream estimators.\nℹ Multivariate specifications are estimated with `estimate_dynes()`."
```

`estimate_dynam()` and `estimate_rem()` abort on a
`joint_specification.goldfish` object -- it is a distinct S3 class that
deliberately does not inherit `specification.goldfish`, so it never reaches
their single-specification dispatch path -- and point to `estimate_dynes()`.
The same estimators (plus `estimate_dynami()`) also abort on a *single*
specification whose focal layer is panel-observed, for the same reason.

When `estimate_dynes()` lands, its viability rule mirrors the separability
rule above: a mixed specification (some fids coupled, some separable)
proceeds, informing which fids could equally be estimated on their own; a
specification where **every** fid is separable -- equivalently, no joined
process's focal layer is a modeled panel process -- aborts, naming
`estimate_dynam()` and explaining that its panel layers would only ever be
static covariates. Construction never makes this call itself: it composes any
valid join and leaves estimability to the consumer, because a fully-separable
join is still a meaningful object for a different consumer -- generative
simulation, next.

# Step 5: Generative-readiness completion

A specification that will *generate* events -- drive the walk handle via a
future `simulate()` or a DyNES augmenter -- or be estimated *jointly* must be
**generatively complete**: every modeled DyNAM flavor needs both a rate and a
choice (REM needs only a rate, already enforced). `make_specification()`
itself no longer aborts on a half-specified flavor (one keyed in `rate` but
not `choice`, or vice versa) so such a specification can still be built and
reach a generative consumer; a *single-process* estimation
(`estimate_dynam()` / `estimate_rem()`) still refuses to estimate the gap, so
rate-only and choice-only single-process models are unaffected.

Filling the gap is a separate, **zero-free-parameter** completion transform
run once at each generative consumer's entry (not part of construction, and
never inside the internal walk handle, which only asserts completeness and
aborts otherwise):

| missing half | default |
|---|---|
| choice | uniform over the support-legal alternatives (no effects) |
| `choice_coordination` | uniform on both sides |
| rate, ordered regime | uniform `rate_ordered` (no effects) |
| rate, timed regime | intercept-only rate, per-actor intercept **pinned** per wave-period from observed counts -- never estimated |

Every default adds *no* parameter to the estimated coefficient vector; the
transform only ever lets a half-specified process reach a generative consumer
without fabricating a scientifically meaningful default. As with
`estimate_dynes()`, no user-facing function calls this transform yet in this
package version -- it is documented here because its contract shapes what a
*complete* joint specification is required to look like once those consumers
land.

# Developer notes: the walk handle

The pieces above build and read a `joint_specification.goldfish`; actually
*preprocessing* it for estimation, or *driving* it forward for simulation or
augmentation, are different jobs. This package version supplies both
substrates internally, for `dynes-augmentation` and `process-simulation` to
build on:

- **Batch preprocessing** (`preprocess_joint()`, internal) walks the composed
  event sequence **once**, on a single shared clock hosting every process's
  statistic blocks, and returns one `preprocessed.goldfish` per fid -- the
  same object shape a single-process `preprocess()` returns, just one per fid
  instead of one for the whole call. An event is dependent for its own
  `(layer, flavor)` fids, a right-censoring boundary for every *other* timed
  rate fid regardless of layer, and state-only for choice/ordered fids --
  cross-process right-censoring works exactly like cross-flavor
  right-censoring in a single flavored specification.

- **The stepping walk handle** (`walk_open()` / `walk_advance()` /
  `walk_evaluate()` / `walk_inject()`, internal, not exported) is for a driver
  that cannot work in one batch pass -- a DyNES augmenter proposing and
  applying latent events mid-walk, or a future `simulate()` drawing new ones.
  It owns the same merged clock and shared process state as the batch walk,
  stepped instead of replayed.

`walk_open(spec, data)` builds the handle. It **asserts** -- never performs --
generative completeness (Step 5): a half-specified spec aborts, pointing at
the consumer that would complete it. `walk_advance(handle, t)` moves the
clock, applying every *exogenous* covariate event (a layer no composed
process models) up to `t`. `walk_evaluate(handle, fid, theta)` returns that
fid's rate vector or choice matrix at the live state and parameters, its
support mask applied -- a thin wrapper over the same process-state evaluators
single-process estimation uses, not a reimplementation. `walk_inject(handle,
event)` applies one event -- observed or sampled -- to the shared state, so
every fid's next evaluation reflects it.

Replaying an observed sequence through advance/evaluate/inject reproduces the
batch walk's per-fid quantities exactly (batch-vs-replay equality); a driver
loop over a proposed sequence looks like this (sketch, not runnable as shown
-- the handle is an internal substrate with no exported entry point):

```r
handle <- walk_open(joint_spec)                 # asserts completeness
for (event in proposed_events) {
  walk_advance(handle, event$time)               # apply exogenous covariates
  rate <- walk_evaluate(handle, fid = rate_fid, theta = theta_rate)
  choice <- walk_evaluate(handle, fid = choice_fid, theta = theta_choice)
  # ... accept/reject or record `rate`/`choice` here ...
  walk_inject(handle, event)                     # commit the event
}
```

Two contracts carry over from the batch walk and matter to anyone driving
the handle: focal is resolved **per fid**, over the one shared state --
  each fid's side/mode/dependent-row resolution rides its own process's
  focal, never a single object-level stamp, so a non-focal process in a
  multilevel join resolves correctly regardless of which layer the data
  object's own `info$focal` happens to name. And a fid carrying an
  auto-supplied, effect-free default (Step 5's uniform choice or pinned rate)
  is a boundary the handle does not yet step past -- those are the generative
  consumers' own domain to walk, not this substrate's.
